✨ Did you know you can make DIY taste-safe kinetic sand with simple ingredients from your pantry? It's non-toxic, budget-friendly, and perfect for toddlers! My 3-year-old often stays busy for an hour playing with it—molding shapes, digging treasures, and pretending to bake "cakes."  Ingredients You’ll Need: 1 cup baking soda 1/2 cup cornstarch 1/2 cup sugar 2–4 tablespoons warm water  (mix with food coloring of your choice) 1 tablespoon cream of tartar Step-by-Step Instructions: Mix the dry ingredients In a large mixing bowl, combine the baking soda, cornstarch, sugar, and cream of tartar. Stir until evenly distributed. Prepare the colored water In a small bowl, add a few drops of food coloring to the warm water. Adjust the intensity of the color by adding more or fewer drops. Combine wet and dry ingredients Gradually add the colored water to the dry mixture, 1 tablespoon at a time. Mix with a spoon or your hands until the sand reaches your desired consistency—moist and moldable, but not sticky. You may not need all the water, so add it slowly! Test and play Once the mixture holds its shape when squeezed, it’s ready for playtime! If it feels too dry, add a few drops of water. If it’s too sticky, sprinkle in a bit more cornstarch. Be sure to follow along for more screen free play ideas and tips to foster independent play skills! 💡 Less screen time, more creativity! 🙌 #sensoryplay #screenfreeactivities #diykidsactivities #toddlermomhacks #tastesafeplay / taste safe sensory play / sensory table ideas

Thomas D. Westergaard is a Danish designer and founder of Ceremoni Studio, where he transforms the traditional candle into a kinetic sculpture. Instead of treating wax as a static object, he engineers candles that bend, twist, and weave together as they burn. Every prototype is tested through long time-lapse recordings to study the flame, the melting wax, and the structure, refining each design until movement and combustion become one. His work sits somewhere between industrial design, engineering, and performance. #art #artist #avantgarde #candles #timelapse

🌈 SUPER SIMPLE TASTE-SAFE KINETIC SAND 🌈 If you’re looking for kid safe kinetic sand - this is it! It might not have the silicone binder that store bought has which gives a stretchy effect, but it’s made with 5 simple ingredients, that still gives it the ability to be squished and moulded while holding its shape and it crumbles like sand. It’s fun, cheap, and so easy to whip up… plus your little ones will love it! INGREDIENTS: 1 cup baking soda 1/2 cup sugar 3/4 cup cornflour  1 Tbsp cream of tartar 1/4 cup of water 1 tsp food colouring (optional) HOW TO: 1. Add the baking soda, sugar, cornflour, and cream of tartar to a large bowl, and stir  everything together. 2. In a small cup, mix your food colouring & water (if you’re using food colouring). 3. Add 2 Tbsp of the water into the dry mix and whisk together. If its still too powdery and doesn’t clump in your hands, add 1 Tbsp more of the water, and stir again. Repeat up to the full 1/4 cup of water, squishing with your hands to mix it in and get the right texture (note if you get heavy handed with the water, counterbalance it by adding equal parts cornflour & sugar, 1 Tbsp of each at a time) 4. Enjoy! NOTES: 🫙 Store in an airtight container in the fridge for 4–6 weeks. If it dries out a little, add 1–2 tsp of water and mix it through with your hands. 🌈  you can make the colour brighter by adding a few extra drops into the water at the beginning. 👶 whilst this recipe is taste-safe, make sure to supervise little ones closely as it’s not for eating by the handful.  . . . . . #kineticsand #toddler #kidsactivities #sensoryplay #playtolearn

Kinetic sculptor Reuben Margolin  creates intricate mechanical installations inspired by mathematics, natural movement, and wave phenomena. Cadence (2024) is a suspended sculpture measuring approximately 3.35 meters in diameter. A single electric motor controls 216 strings connected to an articulated hexagonal lattice made from tapered maple dowels. As the strings move, the wooden structure produces continuous, fluid waves, resembling the movement of water. His Caterpillar Clock (2026) explores a different form of mechanical motion. Built from polished brass, its precisely counterbalanced mechanism uses a small electric motor to move around a large gear, completing one revolution every six minutes. #art #artist #niche #sculpture #design

Artist Rachel Youn creates kinetic sculptures and installations that combine artificial plants, discarded consumer objects and mechanical devices to imitate the movements of living organisms. In Pretty Behavior (2026), Youn modifies a neck massager and connects it to an artificial orchid and leaves using metal hardware, chains and glass. Once activated, the machine makes the flower shake and move continuously, giving the synthetic plant an uncanny appearance of life. Youn frequently repurposes massagers and other machines originally designed to act on the human body, redirecting their repetitive movements into artificial plants. The objects appear to dance, struggle or react despite having no consciousness. #artist #art #niche #weird #avantgarde

In 1970, British artist Peter Logan explored the relationship between movement, rhythm and mechanical precision in 'Square Dance', a fascinating example of early kinetic art, now on view at @Tate Britain. The large-scale mechanical sculpture features four moving arms that perform a repeated sequence of coordinated movements. Rather than remaining a static object, the work becomes a kind of mechanical choreography — a continuous dance governed by motion, timing and repetition. Logan began experimenting with kinetic sculpture in 1968, initially creating electrically powered works that performed aerial movements. His interest in engineering and movement led him to develop sculptures in which mechanical systems become part of the artistic expression. The first version of 'Square Dance' was operated by hand before Logan developed its automated form. Made from aluminium and measuring approximately 2.1 metres high and 3.6 metres across, it entered the Tate collection in 1970. A remarkable encounter between sculpture, engineering and performance, 'Square Dance' reminds us that art does not always need to stand still. . #contemporaryart #exhibition  #KineticArt #TateBritain #MuseumsNews
